prompt: A team says its system has no architecture because nothing was ever designed on purpose. What is the course's answer?

choices.text: Then it has none until somebody documents it
choices.why: A document describes an architecture; it does not create one.

choices.text: It has one; nobody is deciding it
choices.why: Right: structure exists whether chosen or not, and the risk is that it accumulates by accident.

choices.text: It has a design but not an architecture
choices.why: Accidental decisions with high cost of change are architecture whatever their origin.

choices.text: Its architecture is the framework it uses
choices.why: A framework is a technology; lesson 2 separates it from the structure built with it.

prompt: Two services exchange orders. A designer replaces the HTTP call between them with a table both read and write, to avoid timeouts. What changed, in the course's terms?

choices.text: Nothing architectural, since the boxes are the same
choices.why: Same boxes, different connector: a different architecture with different failures.

choices.text: Coupling went down, since there is no call any more
choices.why: Coupling moved into the schema, where every column change now involves both teams.

choices.text: Timeouts traded for coupling through the schema
choices.why: Right: a shared table removes the call failing and adds hidden coupling and lock contention.

choices.text: Only the technology, from HTTP to SQL
choices.why: The technology changed, but so did who knows about whom and what fails together.

prompt: A request passes through four services in a synchronous chain, each available 99.5% of the time. To one decimal place, what percentage of the time does the chain work?
hint: Lesson 1: availabilities in a chain multiply.

prompt: A payments company must show auditors, years later, the exchange rate used in each transfer. Which force of the environment is this, and what does it become?

choices.text: Regulation, becoming data retention
choices.why: Right: the same shape as ANTT's floor table — keep what was in force when the decision was made.

choices.text: Operations, becoming an on-call rota
choices.why: On-call follows from running the system, not from what auditors ask for.

choices.text: The organisation, becoming a team split
choices.why: No team structure is involved; the requirement comes from outside the company.

choices.text: The business, becoming a performance target
choices.why: Speed is not what auditors ask for; they ask for evidence.

prompt: By Booch's definition, a design decision is architectural when it is significant, and significance is measured by its cost of ___.
A company has six teams and one shared service that all of them must change for most features. A year later, the teams queue to deploy it. What does the course call this?

choices.text: An operations failure
choices.why: Deploying is where it shows, but the cause is a structure at odds with the teams.

choices.text: Résumé-driven development
choices.why: Nothing here was chosen for careers; it is a shared component against a team structure.

choices.text: The last responsible moment
choices.why: That concept is about when to decide; this is about a structure bending to the organisation.

choices.text: Conway's law, bending the structure back
choices.why: Right: a structure that ignores the organisation is bent back into its shape, here as a queue of teams.

prompt: An architect is asked to describe a logistics company's architecture and answers "Java, Oracle and Kafka". By the course, what is missing?
hint: Lesson 2, a technology is not an architecture.

choices.text: The versions of each technology
choices.why: Versions make the list longer, not more informative about structure.

choices.text: The elements, how they relate, and what the structure is for
choices.why: Right: the same three tools could build opposite architectures.

choices.text: The cloud provider
choices.why: One more technology on the list still says nothing about structure.

choices.text: Nothing: those are the architectural choices
choices.why: They may be architectural if expensive to change, but they are not a description of the structure.

prompt: A team adds a reporting service nobody planned. It reads only through other services' public APIs and breaks no rule of the intended design. What is that, in the course's terms?
hint: Lesson 2: does it add, or violate?

choices.text: Drift
choices.why: Right: a decision the plan did not include, without contradicting it.

choices.text: Erosion
choices.why: Erosion violates the intended architecture; this service respects it.

choices.text: Big design up front
choices.why: Nothing was designed in advance here; the service arrived unplanned.

choices.text: The descriptive architecture being corrected
choices.why: The descriptive architecture grew; nothing was corrected.

prompt: A team plans to put Kafka in front of a service that receives 40 small writes per second, "for scale". What does the course recommend checking first?

choices.text: Which Kafka distribution to run
choices.why: That chooses the technology before checking whether the number demands it.

choices.text: How the team will learn Kafka
choices.why: Learning is a cost of the solution; first find out whether the solution is needed.

choices.text: Whether the load actually needs a broker
choices.why: Right: 40 small writes a second sits well within a single ordinary database.

choices.text: Whether larger companies run Kafka for similar services
choices.why: Other companies' scale is the Netflix argument the course rejects.

prompt: Order these decisions for a new payments feature from the one whose responsible moment comes first to the one that can wait longest.
items: How a repeated payment request is refused
Which team owns the payments data
Which client library calls the bank
The wording of the confirmation e-mail

prompt: By the course, what is the last responsible moment?

choices.text: The latest date on which a decision can still technically be made
choices.why: That is the last possible moment; the responsible one comes before alternatives are lost.

choices.text: When not deciding would eliminate an important alternative
choices.why: Right: before it you guess, after it the code decides for you.

choices.text: The end of the design phase
choices.why: The course rejects architecture as a phase.

choices.text: The sprint before release
choices.why: It is a property of each decision, not a point in a calendar.

prompt: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows about a running system.
hint: Lesson 2, reading the architecture from the system.

pairs.right: which component can reach which database
which calls actually happen, and in what order
who publishes what, and who listens
which modules depend on which inside one deployable

prompt: A company appoints its first architect and asks what the role is for. Which answer matches the course?
hint: Lesson 3, why Carreto created the role.

choices.text: Reviewing every pull request for quality
choices.why: That makes the architect a bottleneck; reviews belong to the teams.

choices.text: Owning the seams between teams, where nobody was looking
choices.why: Right: structural decisions now happen between teams, where nobody was looking.

choices.text: Choosing the technology stack for each team
choices.why: Inside one team, technology is usually the team's; the architect works across teams.

choices.text: Keeping the architecture diagrams up to date
choices.why: Documentation is part of the job, but a diagram is a view, not the purpose.

prompt: A tech lead is asked to choose the message format two other teams will exchange for years. There is time, and both teams have strong views. Which way of deciding fits best, by the course?

choices.text: She decides alone, to avoid a long debate
choices.why: Deciding alone suits urgency; here there is time and two affected teams.

choices.text: Each team decides and informs the other
choices.why: Two teams deciding separately about one seam is the case the advice process cannot settle.

choices.text: The two teams and the architect decide together
choices.why: Right: expensive to reverse, several teams with conflicting interests, and time to talk.

choices.text: She asks the CTO
choices.why: Escalating avoids the decision rather than choosing how to make it.

prompt: Which of these build earned authority, by the course? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 3, how earned authority is built.

choices.text: Showing the reasoning behind a decision
choices.why: Yes: a reasoning that can be argued with is trusted more.

choices.text: Using the title to settle every disagreement
choices.why: Each use of the title spends earned authority.

choices.text: Saying "I was wrong" quickly when it is true
choices.why: Yes: admitting mistakes builds trust that a title cannot.

choices.text: Making teams faster
choices.why: Yes: involvement that delays a team costs trust even when it is right.

prompt: Under the advice process, a developer decides how her service caches prices, after asking the teams affected. It later causes stale quotes. Who answers for the decision?

choices.text: The architect, who is accountable for all structure
choices.why: The architect answers for the advice given, not for decisions others made.

choices.text: Everyone she consulted
choices.why: Those consulted answer for the quality of their advice, a different obligation.

choices.text: Nobody, since the process was followed
choices.why: Following the process does not remove accountability; it places it.

choices.text: The developer who decided
choices.why: Right: the decider answers, and the two should not be separated.

prompt: Andrew Harmel-Law's practice, in which anyone may make an architectural decision after asking those affected and those with expertise, is called the ___ process.
An architect, asked for a quick answer about retries on a call that moves money to a partner, replies alone in five minutes. What would the course have advised instead?

choices.text: Take it to the people affected before deciding
choices.why: Right: money and an outside system put it at the fourth position, where somebody would ask about duplicates.

choices.text: Answer faster, since quick calls build trust
choices.why: Speed was the cause of the miss, not a remedy for it.

choices.text: Refuse to answer questions about retries
choices.why: Refusing helps nobody; the issue is the way of deciding.

choices.text: Leave it to the junior developer implementing it
choices.why: Moving the decision down without asking those affected repeats the mistake at another desk.

prompt: A bank with five thousand engineers and Carreto with fifty both do enterprise architecture. What differs, by the lesson?

choices.text: Carreto is too small to need any
choices.why: The lesson says Carreto needs a small amount, and Renata builds it.

choices.text: The effort: a department there, a page and a spreadsheet here
choices.why: Right: the questions are the same; the amount of machinery is not.

choices.text: The bank's version looks at years, Carreto's at weeks
choices.why: Both judge enterprise decisions years out.

choices.text: Only the bank maps capabilities to systems
choices.why: Carreto's map was the first thing Renata built at this level.

prompt: What is the horizon of solution architecture?

choices.text: A single sprint
choices.why: One sprint builds a part; the solution's contracts outlive the build.

choices.text: Three to five years
choices.why: That is the enterprise horizon.

choices.text: Months of building, then years running
choices.why: Right: built in weeks or months, and its contracts outlive the code written then.

choices.text: The life of one major version of a service
choices.why: That describes an application decision's horizon.

prompt: The Tracking team wants to split its own database into a table per month to keep queries fast. Nothing it exposes to other systems changes. Which level is that?

choices.text: Application: it stays inside one system
choices.why: Right: the first question passes, so the team decides.

choices.text: Solution, because positions feed the 24-hour payout
choices.why: The payout relies on Tracking's contract, which does not change here.

choices.text: Enterprise, because databases are a company-wide concern
choices.why: One team's internal storage is not a shared platform.

choices.text: It needs Renata's approval before it counts as any level
choices.why: Placing a decision does not depend on who approves it.

prompt: The Shipper team calls Pricing for every quote it shows. What does it need to know about Pricing's architecture?
hint: Lesson 4: the audience of application architecture.

choices.text: The two stages of the quote calculation
choices.why: Those are internals; a caller has no use for them.

choices.text: Which routing provider sits behind the adapter
choices.why: The adapter exists so callers need not know.

choices.text: The full component diagram of the service
choices.why: That is for the team that builds Pricing.

choices.text: The contract and how Pricing behaves when it fails
choices.why: Right: callers need the agreed time or an explicit error, and nothing else.

prompt: Match each level to its time horizon.

pairs.right: months to two years
a programme, then its life
three to five years

prompt: Why does the lesson say solution architecture is where a company of Carreto's size most needs its first architect?
hint: Lesson 4: who was doing each level before Renata?

choices.text: Because enterprise frameworks are too expensive to adopt
choices.why: Cost of frameworks is not the argument.

choices.text: Because the teams design their own services badly
choices.why: The lesson says each team designs its own service well.

choices.text: Nobody owned the journeys between teams
choices.why: Right: application work had owners; the work between teams was being done by nobody.

choices.text: Because solution work is the most senior of the three
choices.why: The levels are not ranks.

prompt: A team must choose a message queue. All candidates handle the load easily. By the lesson, what should decide?
hint: Lesson 5: when fit does not separate the options.

choices.text: The newest release, since it carries the latest ideas
choices.why: Novelty is not among the six questions.

choices.text: Skill, ecosystem, licence, cost and exit
choices.why: Right: when every option fits, the decision is about the team and the company.

choices.text: A benchmark at a hundred times the load
choices.why: Fit is already settled; more fit decides nothing.

choices.text: Whatever the architect used at a previous job
choices.why: Personal history is the enthusiasm the lesson weighed against skill on the team.

prompt: Order an architecture decision record's statuses as one record would pass through them when its decision is later replaced.
In Bezos's terms, a decision that is nearly irreversible is a ___ door.
hint: Lesson 5: you cannot walk back through it.

prompt: An ADR's decision section reads: "An event-driven approach will be adopted for delivery notifications." What is wrong with it, by the lesson?
hint: Lesson 5: a sentence somebody can be held to.

choices.text: It is too short to be a decision
choices.why: Length is not the fault; record 7's decision is short too.

choices.text: It should be in the consequences section
choices.why: A decision belongs in the decision section.

choices.text: Its passive voice hides who does what
choices.why: Right: across teams, who publishes and who consumes is the point.

choices.text: Events are a technology, so they belong in a different log
choices.why: The log records structural choices like this one.

prompt: Why did Renata have the old weekly payout batch written up as record 3, years after it was built?
hint: Lesson 5: a decision about to be changed.

choices.text: So its replacement had something to supersede, with its old reasons
choices.why: Right: it records why the batch was right then, and record 7 points at it.

choices.text: Because every system needs a record before it can be changed
choices.why: The lesson backfills the decisions about to change, not every system.

choices.text: To show the batch was a mistake
choices.why: Record 3 says the batch was correct for the company then.

choices.text: Because finance asked for an audit trail of payouts
choices.why: The reason is the decision log, not an audit request.

prompt: A platform engineer proposes adding approvers, a risk matrix and a diagram slot to every decision record. What does the lesson's reasoning suggest?
hint: Lesson 5: what happens to a record that takes a week to write.

choices.text: Adopt it, since more fields make records more complete
choices.why: Completeness that stops records being written is a loss.

choices.text: Adopt it for one-way doors and two-way doors alike
choices.why: Two-way doors need no record at all.

choices.text: Replace records with design documents
choices.why: Proposals and records do different jobs.

choices.text: Keep records short, or they get written late as paperwork
choices.why: Right: a record written in an afternoon gets written on the day.

prompt: An option scores 4, 3 and 5 on three criteria weighted 50%, 30% and 20%. What is its weighted total?
hint: Lesson 6: sum of weight times score.

prompt: Which of these keep a weighted decision matrix honest, by lesson 6? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 6, the three rules and the constraint.

choices.text: Agreeing the weights before scoring
choices.why: Yes: weights set afterwards drift towards the favourite.

choices.text: Writing a reason beside each score
choices.why: Yes: an unexplained score is a guess.

choices.text: Giving legal requirements the largest weight
choices.why: A legal requirement is a constraint that filters options, not a weight.

choices.text: Scoring cloud bill and running cost as separate criteria
choices.why: That counts one thing twice.

prompt: A team writes: "The search service must be fast." Which rewrite is a quality attribute scenario, by lesson 6?
hint: Lesson 6: six parts, and a measure at the end.

choices.text: The search service must be very fast at peak times, even under heavy load
choices.why: Still adjectives; no measure to test against.

choices.text: A shipper searches loads at the Monday peak; results return within 300 ms for 95% of searches
choices.why: Right: source, stimulus, environment, artefact implied, response and a measure.

choices.text: Search uses an index so it is fast
choices.why: That is a design, not a requirement.

choices.text: Search is as fast as the best competitor's search page on a good day
choices.why: No measure anyone could check on Carreto's system.

prompt: Which of these is a structural decision rather than a technology decision, by lesson 6?
hint: Lesson 6: it would survive swapping the product.

choices.text: Moving logs from one hosted logging vendor to another
choices.why: That swaps a product and leaves the shape alone.

choices.text: Making Tracking the only writer of delivery proofs
choices.why: Right: data ownership, whatever database holds it.

choices.text: Upgrading PostgreSQL to a newer major version
choices.why: A version of a product, not a structure.

choices.text: Choosing a JSON library for Payments
choices.why: A two-way door inside one team.

prompt: A matrix gives option X 3.80 and option Y 3.70. Moving five points of weight between two criteria makes Y win. What should the architect do, by lesson 6?

choices.text: Choose X, since it has the higher total
choices.why: The margin rests on a weight nobody measured.

choices.text: Add criteria until one option clearly leads
choices.why: Adding criteria to manufacture a winner is tuning the matrix.

choices.text: Average X and Y into a hybrid design
choices.why: A hybrid is a third option with its own scores, not a way out of the question.

choices.text: Treat that weight as the question
choices.why: Right: the decision turns on it, so its owners settle that weight, in the open.

prompt: In the 24-hour payout, who owns each side of the contest-window trade-off, by lesson 6?
hint: Lesson 6: name who owns each side.

choices.text: Helena for drivers, Sílvio for the money
choices.why: Right: product speaks for the drivers, finance for the money.

choices.text: Bruno for both, since Payments holds the money
choices.why: Bruno owns preventing duplicates, not the business trade.

choices.text: Renata for both, as the architect
choices.why: She names the owners; she does not become one.

choices.text: The bank partner for speed, Tracking for safety
choices.why: Neither sets the window.

prompt: A product manager writes: "The search must be fast." What is that sentence, as it stands?

choices.text: A functional requirement
choices.why: It says how well, not what.

choices.text: A constraint
choices.why: Nobody outside the product decided it; it is a wish about quality.

choices.text: A quality attribute that is not yet a requirement
choices.why: Right: until it has a number, no design is checkable against it.

choices.text: An architecturally significant requirement
choices.why: Nothing yet says it reshapes the structure.

prompt: A team is asked for "a dashboard for the operations room". After two whys the goal is that late trucks are noticed before the shipper calls. What has happened?
hint: Lesson 7: a request as a solution already chosen.

choices.text: The request gave way to its goal
choices.why: Right: a chosen solution gave way to its problem; noticing late trucks is the requirement, and a dashboard is one way.

choices.text: The request became a constraint
choices.why: Nothing here is imposed from outside.

choices.text: The scope was cut
choices.why: The scope was redirected, not reduced.

choices.text: The root cause of a defect was found
choices.why: No defect was being investigated; the whys found a goal.

prompt: Over a 30-day month, how many minutes of downtime does 99.9% availability allow?
Which requirement is architecturally significant by the lesson's signs?
hint: Lesson 7, the three signs of impact.

choices.text: The confirmation e-mail uses the shipper's logo
choices.why: One team, cheap to change, no measure.

choices.text: A report of bookings per city
choices.why: A report inside one team.

choices.text: Payouts survive the bank partner being down
choices.why: Right: it crosses Payments and the partner, and is expensive to retrofit.

choices.text: The quote page shows the price in reais
choices.why: A display rule for one screen.

prompt: Put the parts of a quality attribute scenario in the order lessons 6 and 7 use.
hint: Who acts, on what, and how it is measured.
trap: The measure comes last because it judges the response.

prompt: An event-storming wall shows support staff re-entering every cancelled booking by hand. What does the lesson say this kind of finding is?

choices.text: A defect to fix before the workshop continues
choices.why: The workshop maps the flow; fixing comes later.

choices.text: A workaround to replace or keep working
choices.why: Right: like the phone calls to drivers, it was invisible to engineering until the wall.

choices.text: A constraint set by support
choices.why: Support did not decide it as a rule; it grew as a workaround.

choices.text: A functional requirement of the support tool
choices.why: It is evidence about the flow, not a feature request.

prompt: A new hire asks for "the architecture diagram" of a 20-service system. What does lesson 8 suggest asking first?

choices.text: Which notation they learnt at university
choices.why: Notation follows from the question.

choices.text: What question they are trying to answer
choices.why: Right: the level of zoom is chosen by the reader's question.

choices.text: Whether they prefer C4 or 4+1
choices.why: A preference for a family does not say which view helps.

choices.text: How many services they have worked with
choices.why: Experience does not pick the view.

prompt: Match each 4+1 view to its concern.

pairs.right: what the system does for its users
what runs at the same time, and under load
how the code is split into modules and teams
what runs on which machines

prompt: Docs as code puts the documentation in the same ___ as the code it describes.
Which documents are records, to be superseded rather than updated? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A postmortem of last month's outage
choices.why: Yes: true as of its date.

choices.text: The container diagram
choices.why: No: it claims to be true now.

choices.text: An ADR choosing Pix for payouts
choices.why: Yes: superseded by a new ADR if the decision changes.

choices.text: A service README with its owner
choices.why: No: a description, kept current.

prompt: Why does a diagram written as text suit code review better than one saved by a drawing tool?

choices.text: It looks better on a slide
choices.why: Autolayout is tidy and rarely beautiful; Renata still draws slides by hand.

choices.text: The line that adds an arrow is the line in the diff
choices.why: Right: a binary or XML file shows only that something changed.

choices.text: Text files are smaller
choices.why: Size is not the reason.

choices.text: Drawing tools are not free
choices.why: Several are free; the issue is reviewing changes.

prompt: An on-call engineer follows a runbook that names a host decommissioned a year ago. In lesson 8's grid, where was the runbook, and which way out fits?

choices.text: Accurate and doubted; nothing to change
choices.why: It was wrong, and she trusted it.

choices.text: Out of date and doubted; it was already harmless
choices.why: She followed it, so it was trusted.

choices.text: Out of date and trusted: fix it or mark it
choices.why: Right: the costly corner, left by fixing it or making it impossible to trust by mistake.

choices.text: Accurate and trusted; the host should be restored
choices.why: The system moved on; the page is what is wrong.

prompt: Carreto's wiki page had 61 rules. Renata deleted 38 and turned 14 into guidelines. How many remained standards?
Put the steps Carreto took to retire the carreto-http rule in order.
items: Announce a date and what replaces the rule
Remove the check on that date
Mark the ADR that introduced it as superseded

prompt: A rule belongs among the standards only if a machine or a reviewer can answer it with yes or ___.
hint: Lesson 9, the test that sorts a standard from a guideline.

prompt: A company publishes a new standard: "Services must be resilient." Applying the lesson's test, what is it?
hint: Lesson 9: can anybody answer yes or no?

choices.text: A strong standard, because it is written with must
choices.why: The word must does not make a rule checkable; two reviewers would disagree on what resilient means.

choices.text: A direction at best, until it is rewritten as a rule with a yes-or-no answer
choices.why: Right: rewritten as, say, a time limit for recovery or a retry rule, it becomes a candidate standard.

choices.text: A guideline, because it uses no numbers
choices.why: Numbers help, but the test is whether a yes or no answer exists.

choices.text: A fitness function, because it is about an architectural characteristic
choices.why: A fitness function is an automated check; this is a sentence nobody can run.

prompt: A team turns on a new dependency check over a codebase that already has 40 violations. Which start does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Fail the build from the first run, so that the 40 are fixed quickly
choices.why: That blocks every team for code most of them did not write, and the check gets switched off.

choices.text: Leave it in report-only mode until the 40 are gone
choices.why: Then new violations keep arriving while the old ones are fixed.

choices.text: Freeze the 40 in a baseline and fail only on new ones
choices.why: Right: the baseline only shrinks, so the code reaches the rule without a week of blocked merges.

choices.text: Fix the 40 first, then write the check
choices.why: Months without a check means new violations arrive faster than old ones leave.

prompt: An exception request answers "until when?" with "when the other team has time". What should the owner of the standard do?
hint: Lesson 9, the three questions before granting.

choices.text: Grant it and renew it later if needed
choices.why: An exception with no real date has nothing for the build to expire on.

choices.text: Ask for a date tied to planned work
choices.why: Right: a date anchored to work already planned is a real one; a wish is not.

choices.text: Refuse it and remove the standard
choices.why: One vague request says nothing about the standard.

choices.text: Grant it without a date, since dates only create pressure
choices.why: Without a date the exception becomes a second, unwritten standard.

prompt: Match each Team Topologies interaction mode to what it looks like.
hint: Lesson 10, the three ways teams work together.

pairs.right: two teams working closely for a while on something new
one team uses another's interface with little talking
one team helps another learn a capability

right_distractors: one team approves the other's designs

prompt: An architect writes a one-page note for the finance director about two structural options. What belongs in it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 10: options in the decider's units.

choices.text: Time and cost of each option, in reais
choices.why: Yes: the decider's units.

choices.text: The risk of each, as fines or delays
choices.why: Yes: risk said as consequences he protects against.

choices.text: The class diagram of the new service
choices.why: Only a technical reader would use it; he needs the consequences.

choices.text: What each option leaves behind for later
choices.why: Yes: what the option enables or costs next year is part of its price.

choices.text: A single recommendation, with no alternatives to distract him
choices.why: A single proposal invites yes or no; options invite a decision.

prompt: The integration manager at Carreto's bank partner can block a go-live but has no interest in how the service is designed. Where on the power and interest grid does she go?

choices.text: Manage closely
choices.why: Her interest in the design is low, so close management would cost her time for nothing.

choices.text: Keep satisfied
choices.why: Right: high power, low interest, like the accounting firm in the lesson.

choices.text: Keep informed
choices.why: That corner is for those with low power; she can block the go-live.

choices.text: Monitor
choices.why: Monitoring someone who can stop the launch is how a go-live gets blocked by surprise.

prompt: Two teams both change a shared notification module, and most of its incidents start where one team's change breaks the other's assumption. What does the lesson's approach suggest?

choices.text: A review step in which both teams approve each change to the module
choices.why: Two approvals keep the seam inside the module and add a queue.

choices.text: Rewrite it as a microservice owned jointly
choices.why: Joint ownership is what produced the incidents.

choices.text: One team owns it, and the other asks for changes through an interface it keeps
choices.why: Right: the managers arrange the ownership and the code follows.

choices.text: More tests on the module, written by the architect
choices.why: Tests help, but the cause is two owners each assuming different things.

prompt: A product manager asks for a feature that, unknown to her, breaks an assumption four teams rely on. What is the architect's first move, by the lesson?
hint: Lesson 10, the page Renata wrote for Helena.

choices.text: Refuse until the structure has been refactored
choices.why: That is the architect who says no, and product learns to route around him.

choices.text: Build it quietly and absorb the extra cost
choices.why: The structure pays silently, which is the other failure.

choices.text: Take it to the CTO to decide
choices.why: The priority is product's; the architect's job is the information.

choices.text: Write options with cost and risk; she chooses
choices.why: Right: options in her units, including what each leaves behind.

prompt: A company's architecture review board approves every design, and teams now bring it decisions they have already made. What change does the lesson point to?
hint: Lesson 10, a forum and not a board.

choices.text: Advise; the proposer decides
choices.why: Right: advice draws proposals early, while they can still change; the advice is recorded in the ADR.

choices.text: Meet more often so that the queue moves faster
choices.why: A faster queue is still a queue, and decisions still arrive made.

choices.text: Require slides so proposals are better prepared
choices.why: The forum's rule is no slides; the time is for questions.

choices.text: Make attendance mandatory for every tech lead
choices.why: Attendance is not the measure; which teams bring proposals is.

prompt: Paula, on Platform, tells the architect she wants to add a second database for build logs because "the current one is struggling". What should the architect's first question be about, according to lesson 11?
hint: Lesson 11, the first of the four questions.

choices.text: Which database product Platform has in mind
choices.why: That starts from the solution. The lesson asks for the goal and the number first.

choices.text: The measurement behind "struggling", and the target
choices.why: Right: a clarifying question turns "struggling" into a number to move, which every later question is tested against.

choices.text: Whether the standard on databases allows a second one for Platform
choices.why: Pointing at a standard is a different hat, and it comes after understanding the problem.

choices.text: Who on Platform will be on call for the new database at night
choices.why: A fair cost to raise later, but it presumes the database is the answer.

prompt: An architect is convinced that a team's design will fail at the Monday peak. Which way of saying so fits lesson 11?
hint: Lesson 11, the leading question and the three hats.

choices.text: "Have you considered what happens on Monday mornings?", and wait for them to see it
choices.why: When the architect already holds the answer, a question like this becomes a guessing game, which the lesson calls leading.

choices.text: Approve it and let the team learn from the incident
choices.why: Letting a known failure ship is not teaching; the lesson's practice-without-stakes is the kata, not production.

choices.text: State the view and the reason, call it advice, and say who decides
choices.why: Right: an honest view, labelled with the hat being worn, keeps the decision where the advice process puts it.

choices.text: Block it at the forum until the team adopts the architect's design
choices.why: That takes the decision away while pretending to advise, and turns the forum into a gate.

prompt: The Shipper team's design lets shippers cancel a load after a driver has accepted it, and its measure is that the driver is told within one minute. Which review comments deserve the label "blocking"? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 11: blocking means unsafe, or missing the stated measure.

choices.text: Notifications are sent once a minute in a batch, so a driver hears after up to two
choices.why: Yes: the design misses its own stated measure.

choices.text: I would name the endpoint /loads/{id}/cancel rather than /loads/{id}/void
choices.why: Wording, so a nit.

choices.text: If the cancel and the driver's pickup arrive together, both are accepted
choices.why: Yes: an unsafe race, found by asking what happens when two parts act at once.

choices.text: Have you considered using the broker instead of an HTTP call here?
choices.why: A suggestion or a question, unless the HTTP call fails a stated requirement.

prompt: Match each review label to what it asks of the author.

pairs.right: fix it before the design is accepted
explain, and the answer decides what follows
consider it; the author decides
ignore it freely

prompt: In a design, the Driver app uploads a delivery photo to delivery-proof and then calls the monolith to mark the delivery complete. Which question belongs to a failure walk?
hint: Lesson 11: every box and every arrow, asking how it fails.

choices.text: Is the photo stored as JPEG or as a more modern format?
choices.why: A detail of one box, not a failure.

choices.text: Who owns delivery-proof, and how often is it deployed?
choices.why: Useful for an inventory, not for asking how this flow fails.

choices.text: What happens if the upload succeeds and the call to the monolith fails?
choices.why: Right: it asks about the arrow between two parts, the case where one step happened and the next did not.

choices.text: Could the app show a nicer screen while the photo uploads?
choices.why: A product question about the happy path.

prompt: During a kata presentation, a participant says "I would have used Postgres" about another group's design. What does lesson 11 say about comments like this?
hint: Lesson 11, the two rules for katas.

choices.text: They are the point of the kata, since each group defends its tools
choices.why: The discussion is about reasoning, not about defending a favourite tool.

choices.text: Question the trade-off instead, unless the tool changes one
choices.why: Right: the rule is to question trade-offs, not boxes; a tool preference matters only when it changes a trade-off.

choices.text: Ban technology names from katas so groups draw only abstract boxes
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson removes technology from a design; it redirects the questions.

choices.text: Answer it by checking which group's design the architect prefers
choices.why: There is no correct answer to find in a kata, which is deliberate.

prompt: After its clean-up Carreto runs 10 deployable services, and Platform's figure for routine upgrades is 6 hours per service per month. How many hours a month of upgrade work remain?
hint: Lesson 12, the cost of keeping a service.

prompt: Brooks called the complexity that belongs to the problem itself, and survives any choice of tools, ___ complexity.
The Driver team proposes a new service that formats SMS texts, called by notifications and by nothing else. What does lesson 12's inventory suggest?
hint: Lesson 12, the pattern in the five.

choices.text: Build it: small services are easier to understand than modules
choices.why: A small deployable still carries a pager, upgrades and somebody's memory every month.

choices.text: Keep it in notifications: one caller buys no independence and costs every month
choices.why: Right: a service with one caller has none of the benefits of a service and all of its monthly costs.

choices.text: Build it, but give it to Platform so Driver carries no on-call
choices.why: Moving the cost to another team does not remove it.

choices.text: Ask product whether shippers use the SMS texts
choices.why: Whether the feature exists is not in question; whether it needs its own deployable is.

prompt: To ship a report in an hour, a team adds a column to a table that three other teams also read and write. On Hickey's two axes, where does the change sit?

choices.text: Simple and easy: one column, one hour
choices.why: Easy, yes. But it ties four teams' changes to one table, which is the opposite of simple.

choices.text: Easy, and complex
choices.why: Right: close at hand today, and one more braid between four teams from then on.

choices.text: Simple, and hard at first
choices.why: It was not hard; an hour is why it was chosen.

choices.text: Neither: a column is too small to have a place on the axes
choices.why: Every choice sits somewhere on both axes. Small changes are where most braids come from.

prompt: By Dan McKinley's argument, where should a company spend its few innovation tokens?

choices.text: On whichever team asks first, to reward initiative
choices.why: The tokens are spent by the whole company, which pays the operating cost.

choices.text: On the newest tools, so the company stays attractive to hire into
choices.why: That spends tokens for reasons unrelated to the business, which is the case McKinley argues against.

choices.text: Where the company is trying to be different from others
choices.why: Right: novelty is worth its unknown failure modes where it is the business's advantage; elsewhere, boring technology.

choices.text: On infrastructure only, since business code is better kept boring
choices.why: The rule is about where the company differs, not about which layer of the stack.

prompt: An internal service has shown no traffic for three days, and its team wants to delete its repository and alerts this afternoon. What does lesson 12 advise?

choices.text: Go ahead: three days of silence is proof enough
choices.why: A fortnightly job nobody remembered would not show up in three days.

choices.text: Keep it running for good, since removal is risky
choices.why: Keeping it has a monthly cost; the steps exist to make removal safe, not to avoid it.

choices.text: Delete the alerts now and the repository next quarter
choices.why: A half-removed service is worse than either; deletion is the last step, done whole.

choices.text: Two silent weeks, a month switched off, then delete it all
choices.why: Right: watch for two weeks, switch off but keep it switchable for a month, then delete everything it left behind.

prompt: Using n(n − 1) / 2, how many pairs of people have to keep in step in a team of 6?
Put the parts of a debt register entry in the order Renata wrote them in lesson 13.
hint: Lesson 13: from what was borrowed to when to look again.
trap: Writing the repayment before the interest leaves the reader without the reason the repayment is worth its cost.

prompt: Which of these pieces of work at Carreto deserves the highest quality bar, by lesson 13's test?
hint: Lesson 13: lifetime, rate of change, and what being wrong costs.

choices.text: A script that renames old files once, rehearsed on a copy
choices.why: It runs once, and being wrong costs a rerun.

choices.text: The code that keeps every quote above the ANTT floor
choices.why: Right: it lives for years, changes weekly, and being wrong is a breach of the law with Carreto's name on it.

choices.text: An internal page listing this week's on-call engineers
choices.why: A wrong entry is noticed and fixed by a person in minutes.

choices.text: A prototype for next month's kata
choices.why: It lives an afternoon and costs nothing when wrong.

prompt: Carreto's bank partner announces a new Pix API, with the old one switched off on a fixed date eight weeks away. Two engineers on Payments know the payout code. Following lesson 13, what should the plan move?
hint: Lesson 13, a date nobody can move.

choices.text: The date, by asking the bank for an exception
choices.why: The date belongs to the bank, as the CT-e's belonged to the tax authority.

choices.text: Cost, by adding four engineers from other teams
choices.why: People who do not know the payout code would slow the two down, which is Brooks's law.

choices.text: Scope: what must work on the day, and what waits
choices.why: Right: with the date and the team fixed, scope is the corner left, and each item is asked what happens on the day if it is not done.

choices.text: Internal quality, by skipping tests on the new client
choices.why: Payouts move money; the bar stays full for what ships on the day.

prompt: By lesson 13, what is the architect's part when quality, time and cost pull apart?
hint: Lesson 13, three options and who chooses.

choices.text: Recommend, spell out consequences, record it
choices.why: Right: the business decides; the architect makes the decision informed and writes the debt down.

choices.text: Decide how good the engineering must be and defend it
choices.why: One of the two habits lesson 13 names, and it takes the decision from the people who own the time and money.

choices.text: Accept the date and absorb the difference quietly
choices.why: The other habit: it hides the consequences until they arrive.

choices.text: Present the engineers' preferred option and its cost
choices.why: One option is a request for approval; the decider learns nothing about the alternatives.

prompt: A manager says: "Design stamina means we must never cut corners, not even on a two-day prototype we will throw away." What does lesson 13 say?
hint: Lesson 13, where the payoff line falls.

choices.text: He is right: internal quality is never the variable to trade
choices.why: That holds for code that will change again. A throwaway's life ends before the line.

choices.text: He is right for code with tests, and wrong for code without
choices.why: The distinction lesson 13 draws is about the code's lifetime, not whether it has tests yet.

choices.text: Cutting pays for a real throwaway
choices.why: Right: a prototype that is truly thrown away never reaches the crossing, so skimping on it costs nothing later.

choices.text: Design stamina only applies to projects longer than a year
choices.why: Fowler puts the crossing within weeks, which is why most code is past it.

prompt: A product manager asks an architect in a lift how long a new search feature will take, and the architect says "six weeks". Ten minutes later the number is in a roadmap. What went wrong?

choices.text: An estimate without a range was read as a commitment
choices.why: Right: a number said in a corridor becomes a commitment the moment somebody writes it down.

choices.text: The architect should have answered in hours, not weeks
choices.why: Hours suggest a precision nobody has at that stage; the unit is not the problem.

choices.text: The product manager set a target too early
choices.why: She asked for an estimate; the target appeared only when the number was written into the roadmap.

choices.text: Six weeks was too pessimistic for a search feature
choices.why: Nobody can tell from the lift whether it was too high or too low, which is the point.

prompt: A data migration is estimated at O = 4, M = 6 and P = 14 days. What is its PERT mean, in days?
Carreto buys insurance that pays out if a fraud ring is paid by mistake. Which response to the risk is that?

choices.text: Avoid
choices.why: Avoiding changes the plan so the risk cannot happen; the fraud is still possible here.

choices.text: Reduce
choices.why: Reducing lowers the likelihood or Carreto's own impact through its own actions, such as a cap.

choices.text: Accept
choices.why: Accepting means living with the consequence; here somebody else pays it.

choices.text: Transfer
choices.why: Right: the consequence moves to somebody better placed to carry it, for a price.

prompt: Put the stages of a project in the order the cone of uncertainty narrows through them, widest first.
trap: The order is set by decisions taken, not by time spent: a project that waits without deciding stays at the wide end.

prompt: Two options are compared: build a reporting service in-house, or buy one. The comparison table has no row for keeping today's spreadsheets. What does that hide?

choices.text: The licence cost of the bought service
choices.why: That cost would be on the buy row; the missing row is a different one.

choices.text: Whether either beats standing still
choices.why: Right: without the baseline, the table makes one of the two look inevitable.

choices.text: The exit cost of building in-house
choices.why: Exit cost belongs in the rows that are there; it is not what a missing option hides.

choices.text: Which team would own the new service
choices.why: Ownership matters, but it is a property of the two options, not of the absent one.

prompt: A team's estimate for a search index runs from 2 to 12 weeks because nobody knows whether the current database can serve the queries. What is the cheapest next step?

choices.text: Plan at 12 weeks to be safe
choices.why: Planning at the pessimistic end pays for the uncertainty instead of removing it.

choices.text: Average the two ends and plan at 7 weeks
choices.why: Averaging hides the open question, which is still there on day one of the work.

choices.text: A short, time-boxed spike against the database
choices.why: Right: a few days that answer the question narrow the range more than any arithmetic.

choices.text: A pre-mortem with the whole team
choices.why: A pre-mortem questions a chosen plan; here the plan is not chosen and the question is technical.

prompt: An architect who last opened the repository a year ago reviews a design and calls it "a two-week job". The team says two months. By lesson 15, what is the likeliest explanation?

choices.text: The team is protecting itself with a long estimate
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson's first suspect is the reading of somebody away from the code for a year.

choices.text: His sense of the cost drifted
choices.why: Right: experience decays when it stops being renewed, and drift is felt by nobody.

choices.text: The design is wrong and should be rejected
choices.why: Nothing says the design is wrong; it may only be mispriced.

choices.text: Two months is the time a review takes
choices.why: The estimate is for building, not for reviewing.

prompt: Alistair Cockburn's name for a tiny version of the system that runs one small function end to end, through every main part, is the ___ skeleton.
hint: Lesson 15, the figure with one line through every box.

prompt: Match each author to the idea the course takes from them.

pairs.right: Architectus oryzus, who mentors rather than decides alone
the architect riding between penthouse and engine room
the walking skeleton
the pre-mortem

prompt: Which of these suit an architect's two half-days a week, by lesson 15? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A fitness function for a rule the architect set
choices.why: Yes: off every critical path by construction, and it keeps working in meetings.

choices.text: The last story before a release
choices.why: The release would wait on an interrupted calendar.

choices.text: A slow query from a team's backlog, chosen with that team
choices.why: Yes: a small fix in the real code, which nobody is waiting for.

choices.text: A three-day spike on a library's behaviour under load
choices.why: Yes: a question the architect has asked, answered inside a time box.

choices.text: Sole ownership of the migration's core module
choices.why: That is the critical path again; pairing with the owner is the alternative.

prompt: A team waves the architect's pull requests through without comments. By lesson 15, what is lost?

choices.text: Nothing, since the architect's code is reviewed by the architect
choices.why: Self-review is not the team's review, and the lesson asks for the team's.

choices.text: Speed, because reviews slow the architect down
choices.why: The architect's code is off the critical path, so review costs no release anything.

choices.text: The review, and the message that conventions bind her too
choices.why: Right: a team that does not review her is not reviewing, and the juniors learn rank instead.

choices.text: Her authority, since unreviewed code looks careless
choices.why: The loss is to the team's habits, more than to how she looks.

prompt: An architect can no longer run the company's system on a laptop from a clean checkout. By lesson 15, what is the cheapest response?
hint: Lesson 15: most of the five questions have the same answer.

choices.text: Ask Platform for a hosted environment to use instead
choices.why: That works around the symptom and leaves her outside the code the team runs.

choices.text: Change something small in the code this week
choices.why: Right: getting the setup running again is the first step of that change, and it recalibrates.

choices.text: Accept it as a normal part of seniority
choices.why: The lesson accepts coding less, never stopping; this is a sign of drift.

choices.text: Read the onboarding document again
choices.why: Reading tells her how it was meant to work; changing something tells her how it works now.

prompt: A company rewards its best senior engineer by naming her architect, calling it "the next rung". Which idea from lesson 16 does that framing miss?

choices.text: That architects are paid less than senior engineers
choices.why: Pay is not what the lesson discusses.

choices.text: That the new job is a different scope and horizon, not more of the old one
choices.why: Right: changing role swaps one box for another, and some of what made her good will not help.

choices.text: That architects stop writing code once named
choices.why: Lesson 15 argues the opposite.

choices.text: That the title has to come with a team to manage
choices.why: The architect manages nobody, by lesson 16's last section.

prompt: A staff engineer spends a year running the CTO's reorganisation of three departments, deciding in her name. Which of Larson's archetypes fits?

choices.text: Solver
choices.why: A solver goes deep into hard technical problems; this is acting for an executive.

choices.text: Architect
choices.why: The architect answers for an area of the system over time, with authority of their own.

choices.text: Tech lead of the three departments
choices.why: A tech lead guides one team's approach and execution.

choices.text: Right hand
choices.why: Right: she extends the CTO's reach with his scope and authority.

prompt: Under Carreto's decision-rights table, Matching wants to keep a copy of the drivers' bank details that Payments holds. Who decides?

choices.text: Matching's tech lead, since the copy would live in Matching's database
choices.why: Where the copy lives does not change whose data it is.

choices.text: Payments' tech lead, as the owner of the original
choices.why: He must be asked; the table gives data ownership to the architect.

choices.text: The architect, after asking both tech leads
choices.why: Right: who owns which data and who may read it is one of her two rows.

choices.text: Platform, because a copy needs replication
choices.why: Platform may be asked about the mechanism; the ownership question is not theirs.

prompt: An architect proposes to review every pull request: 300 a week at 9 minutes each. How many hours a week is that?
hint: Lesson 16. Minutes in total, divided by 60.

prompt: Which of these lie outside the architect's role, by lesson 16? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Deciding which feature the Shipper team builds next
choices.why: Yes: product priorities are Helena's.

choices.text: Holding the ticket a team's release depends on
choices.why: Yes: the architect stays off the critical path.

choices.text: Deciding whether a new database goes into production
choices.why: That row is the architect's.

choices.text: Choosing who is promoted on the Tracking team
choices.why: Yes: promotions belong to the engineering manager.

choices.text: Keeping the standards and their automated checks
choices.why: Standards and their enforcement stay inside the boundary (lesson 9).

prompt: Which question is the tech lead the one person on a team to answer, by lesson 16?

choices.text: How does this team build what it has to build?
choices.why: Right: the team's internal design and the way it works on the code.

choices.text: What does the company build next year?
choices.why: That is product's, at company scope.

choices.text: Who owns the data that is shared between several teams?
choices.why: Data ownership across teams is the architect's row.

choices.text: Who on the team gets a raise this year?
choices.why: Pay and promotion are the engineering manager's.

prompt: An architect publishes a rule that all front-end code must use one state library, decided with the platform team alone. Within a quarter, four of five front-end teams have exceptions. Which antipattern, and what was the alternative?
hint: Lesson 17, the memo and its exceptions.

choices.text: The gatekeeper; review each team's code for the library
choices.why: Reviewing everyone's code is the gatekeeper itself, not a cure for a decision taken without the teams.

choices.text: The ivory tower; seek the affected teams' advice before deciding
choices.why: Right: the advice process, with the exceptions' reasons arriving before the rule instead of after.

choices.text: Overengineering; use no state library
choices.why: The fault is in how the rule was made, not in the size of the design.

choices.text: The PowerPoint architect; draw the rule on a diagram
choices.why: A drawing of the rule would not have asked anybody anything.

prompt: A platform team builds a multi-cloud abstraction layer so that the company "could move off its cloud provider". No move is planned, and every service now pays a layer of indirection. Which antipattern is it?

choices.text: The absent architect
choices.why: Somebody designed a great deal here, on purpose.

choices.text: Overengineering
choices.why: Right: building for a problem the company does not have, paid by every service.

choices.text: The ivory tower
choices.why: Nothing says the teams were not asked; the problem is the size of the answer.

choices.text: The PowerPoint architect
choices.why: The layer was built and runs; it is not a drawing that the code fails to match.

prompt: A company has no architect. Each team picked its own way to authenticate service calls, and there are now four. A security review asks which one is the standard. What does lesson 17 say the alternative would have been?

choices.text: A central team that approves every service-to-service call
choices.why: That trades the absent architect for the gatekeeper.

choices.text: A complete security architecture written before any service is built
choices.why: Big design up front is the other extreme lesson 2 warned about.

choices.text: An owner for that cross-team decision, and a record of it
choices.why: Right: decision rights plus a decision record, just enough design for what crosses teams.

choices.text: Letting the four approaches compete until one wins on its own
choices.why: That is the accident continuing; nothing decides, so nothing wins.

prompt: Put the parts of the lesson's analysis of each antipattern in the order it uses them.
hint: Lesson 17: what you see, then why, then the bill, then the way out.

prompt: Lesson 17's one question for telling a drawing from a wish: can the person who drew this arrow point to the ___ where it lives?
Match each antipattern to the alternative lesson 17 gives for it.

pairs.right: draw what exists, dated, beside the code
run the decision through the advice process
automate the checkable rules and review only what crosses teams
design for the measured need and record what was not built
